summary: This is a logging library for Bash scripts that provides functions to write timestamped log entries to a file. When sourced into another script, it sets up a temporary log file, captures function call traces, and automatically displays the log contents when the script exits. The library is designed to be included in other scripts via `source log.sh` and used by calling `log::write` with a message.

explanations.19: This tells Bash to immediately exit if any variable used hasn't been defined, catching typos and mistakes early.
explanations.20: This tells Bash to immediately exit if any command fails, rather than continuing with the rest of the script.
explanations.44: This registers a function to run automatically when the script exits, letting us clean up the log file before the program ends.
explanations.48: This checks if LOG_FILE hasn't been set yet; if not, it creates a unique temporary filename like `/tmp/myScript.sh.ABC123.log` using mktemp.
explanations.51: This defines a nested function that outputs the current date and time in ISO format whenever called.
explanations.60: BASH_LINENO is a special array that tracks line numbers of the call stack; this gets its length to know how many nested function calls there are.
explanations.62: The loop skips index 0 and 1 (which are internal to the logging functions) and walks through the rest of the call stack to build a trace.
explanations.63: This appends each function name and its line number to build a chain showing which functions called which, in reverse order.
explanations.66: This removes the trailing semicolon from the trace string using sed so it looks clean.
explanations.74: This opens file descriptor 3 and points it to the log file; later, `>&3` will write to this log file instead of stdout.
explanations.98: The `-s` test checks if the file exists AND has content (is not empty).
explanations.135: If LOG_FILE is empty or unset, there's nowhere to log, so return early to skip all the work.
explanations.137: This creates a read-only variable holding the first argument passed to the function, or an empty string if nothing was passed.
explanations.138: If no message was provided as an argument, there's nothing to log, so return early.
explanations.141: This creates the log file if it doesn't exist yet, but skips creation if LOG_FILE is `/dev/stdout` (a special case for terminal output).
explanations.144: This checks if the log file exists but isn't writable, which would prevent logging.
explanations.150: The `-s` test checks if the file is empty; if it is, write a startup message before the first real log entry.
explanations.154: This writes the actual log entry with a timestamp, the message, and a function call trace to file descriptor 3 (the log file).
explanations.178: The `-s` test checks if the log file has content; if it's empty, skip displaying it.
explanations.184: This prints an ANSI escape code to change text color to gray before displaying the log content.
explanations.185: This uses sed to strip out ANSI color codes from the log file so the display is clean (removes escape sequences like `[31m`).
explanations.195: This tries to return from the script as if it were sourced; a sourced script succeeds, but running it directly fails, so this detects which happened.
explanations.196: If sourcing failed (sourced=0), the script was run directly instead of sourced, which is an error.
explanations.201: Now that the file is sourced, call the initialization function to set up all the logging infrastructure.
